sketch.caption: The article is a chain: it starts from a problem classical synapse-only models can't solve, builds up a wave-based control mechanism step by step, and ends by using that mechanism to explain consciousness and rival theories.

scenes.title: From a problem to a theory of consciousness

items.text: Synapses alone can't explain flexible top-down control
Classical view: fixed, specialized neurons
items.detail: Hierarchical feedforward circuits with stable neuron 'meanings'.

items.text: Neurons are multifunctional: mixed selectivity
Brain waves organize & route spiking
Waves directly shift spiking via ephaptic coupling
Alpha/beta 'stencils' gate gamma/spiking
Explains mixed selectivity & subspace coding
Traveling waves drive shifts between coding states
Wave interference = analog computation
Hybrid synapse/wave framework of consciousness

scenes.caption: Each stage solves a gap left by the one above it, ending in a framework that explains both anesthesia and consciousness theories.

scenes.title: Inside Spatial Computing theory

items.text: Alpha/beta rhythms act as inhibitory 'stencils' over cortex
They suppress gamma/spiking in targeted locations
Confirmed in primate prefrontal cortex; predicts errors
Alpha/beta's mid spatial scale suits top-down control
Explains mixed selectivity: same neuron gated differently by context
Explains subspace coding: gating creates orthogonal population subspaces

scenes.caption: A funnel: one mechanism (alpha/beta stencils gating gamma) narrows down to explain two separate puzzling observations in neural data.

scenes.title: Inside the consciousness argument

items.text: Anesthetics from different drug classes all converge on slow, desynchronized waves
Synapses store info; waves decide what's active now, binding distributed activity
vs Global Workspace / IIT: integration via fields, not broadcast or a 'hot zone'
vs Higher-Order theories: top-down organization itself is the conscious act
Consciousness depends on wave organization, not specific circuits
Conclusion: brain-wide wave dynamics efficiently organize cognition & consciousness

scenes.caption: A converge: evidence from anesthesia and comparisons with rival theories both feed into the same final claim about wave-based consciousness.

plates.title: From Tangled Wires to One Glowing Brain
plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript page on aged cream parchment, sepia ink outlines with muted watercolour washes of indigo, ochre and dull red, gold leaf reserved for the final scene only. Ten framed vignettes run top to bottom in a single reading column, each in its own small arched panel bordered by a thin ink rule, with a short capitalised title lettered beneath each panel in plain serif capitals — no other words appear anywhere on the page. At the top, a robed overseer-figure stands helpless before a tangle of threads running to tiny bells (THE OVERSEER AND THE TANGLED THREADS). Below it the path forks: to the left, a single side-panel shows lines assembling upward into a cat through paw, nose, whisker stages (LINES BUILT INTO A CAT), a dead branch that does not continue downward; to the right the main column continues with a single neuron-bell ringing for one object only when it comes first in a short sequence, silent when it comes second (THE BELL THAT CHANGES ITS MIND). The column continues down into a drawn enclosure (a double ink border) holding two panels together: shuttered windows along a corridor opening and closing in sequence (WINDOWS OPENING IN TURN), and branching Purkinje-like cells radiating rings that pull neighbours into step with no wires drawn (TREES THAT SYNCHRONIZE WITHOUT WIRES). Below this enclosure, a second framed enclosure holds two more panels: a hand laying a cut stencil over a cortex sheet so light shows only through the gaps (THE STENCIL LAID OVER THE BRAIN), and the same bell-neuron lit differently under two different stencils (TWO STENCILS, ONE BELL). The column narrows further into a single ribbon of wave-crests sweeping diagonally across a cortical sheet, leaving a rippled trail (THE SWEEPING RIBBON OF WAVES), then an old brass wheel-and-disk machine overlaid faintly with crossing wave-ripples (THE TIDE-PREDICTING MACHINE). The page ends at the bottom in the only panel touched with gold leaf: a baker sliding synaptic-tree-shaped loaves into a glowing oven, the loaves emerging patterned like the waves above, beneath one whole brain lit gold (BAKING THE WORLD INTO WIRING). Thin ink arrows connect each panel to the next down the page, forking once near the top and rejoining into the single descending chain.

plates.title: The Stencil's Two Shadows
plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript page, same aged parchment and sepia-ink register as the overview, with muted indigo, ochre and dull red washes and no gold leaf. Six framed panels run top to bottom in a narrowing funnel shape, each with a capitalised title lettered beneath it and no other words on the page. At the very top, opening the plate, sits the same stencil-over-cortex scene from the overview (THE STENCIL LAID OVER THE BRAIN), signalling this plate is the inside of that scene. Below it, a single panel shows two opposing wave-patterns, one tight and fast and one broad and slow, pulling against each other like a taut rope across the cortical sheet (TUG-OF-WAR OF TWO RHYTHMS). Below that, a monkey seated at a small table of objects wears a shifting glow across its brow, the glow's pattern briefly mismatched to mark an error (THE MONKEY'S MISMATCHED PATTERN). Below that, a small ruler lies across the cortical sheet marking a span of a few finger-widths, with tight fine ripples shown beneath it and one broader ripple matching its span above it (THE RIGHT-SIZED RULER). The column then forks into two panels side by side at the bottom of the page, each occupying half the page's width so the funnel visibly widens again at its mouth: on the left, the same bell-neuron lit differently under two different stencils (TWO STENCILS, ONE BELL); on the right, a scattered cloud of small points collapsing onto a single curved ribbon-sheet floating inside a larger open cube (THE CLOUD COLLAPSED TO A RIBBON). Thin ink arrows run down the single column from panel to panel and split into the two side-by-side panels only at the very end, making the narrowing-then-forking funnel shape plain. Vignettes are drawn large enough to fill most of the page's width, with only a thin undecorated parchment margin left bare at the outer edges.

plates.title: Four Roads to One Light
plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript page in the same aged parchment, sepia ink and muted wash register as the earlier plates, with gold leaf reserved only for the final panel. Four framed panels sit in a row across the upper half of the page, each roughly a quarter of the page's width so all four are visible together: a set of three vials pouring different coloured streams that bend together into one flat slow wave over a dimmed brain (THREE VIALS, ONE SLOW WAVE); loose coloured threads across a cortical sheet gathered by a wave-line into one glowing braided cord (THE SCATTERED THREADS WOVEN TOGETHER); a small fiery red patch on a brain outline crossed through beside a broad cool ripple spreading across the whole surface (NOT A HOT ZONE, BUT A WIDE RIPPLE); and an upper tier of overlapping wave-rings pressing a grid-stencil of order down onto a busier layer of small spiking marks (THE UPPER WAVE PRESSING ORDER DOWN). Thin ink arrows run down from all four panels, converging into a single wide panel that spans the full width of the page below them: small receptor shapes fading to pale outlines while one unbroken wave pattern glows intact across the whole cortical sheet behind them (THE RECEPTORS FADE, THE WAVE HOLDS). From this panel a single arrow continues down to the final panel at the foot of the page, the only one touched with gold leaf: the entire brain outline glowing evenly under one sweeping wave pattern reaching every part of its surface at once (THE WHOLE BRAIN LIT AS ONE). Capitalised titles are lettered beneath each panel in plain serif capitals; no other words appear anywhere on the page. The four upper panels and the convergence panel below them are grouped by a shared thin double-ink border drawn around all five, visually marking them as one gathering stage before the final solitary panel.

occurrences.reasoning: Applies the wave-summation computation idea to a concrete cognitive example of combining two contexts.

ideas.name: Unconsciousness reflects loss of large-scale wave organization, not any one drug target
ideas.statement: Chemically unrelated anesthetics all end up producing the same breakdown into slow, poorly coordinated cortical waves, suggesting that consciousness depends on the integrity of large-scale wave organization rather than on any specific receptor or cell type.

occurrences.quote: Despite acting on different molecular targets, different anesthetic agents, such as propofol (GABAergic), ketamine (NMDAergic), and dexmedetomidine (alpha-2 adrenergic), all converge on similar large-scale electrical effects in the cortex
occurrences.reasoning: Shows that diverse molecular mechanisms converge on the same systems-level wave disruption, the key evidence for the claim.

occurrences.quote: These slow waves are often temporally misaligned, disrupting coordinated communication. The result may be a destabilized, fragmented cortex.
occurrences.reasoning: Specifies what breaks down (coordination across the cortex) rather than any local circuit property.

occurrences.quote: This suggests that consciousness depends less on specific receptors or cell types and more on the integrity of large-scale wave organization.
occurrences.reasoning: States the conclusion directly, generalizing from the convergence of unrelated drugs to a claim about what consciousness requires.

quotes.text: Cognition and consciousness may arise from bidirectional interactions between neuron spiking and large-scale brain waves. We propose that, while synapses store memories, brain waves provide an executive-like control process that organizes millions of neurons into lower-dimensional, coordinated patterns in real time.
quotes.reason: States the paper's central thesis

quotes.text: However, synaptic changes are likely too cumbersome for flexible top-down control. That would require a control system to “know” which synapses and neurons were employed for any given neural representation and selectively coordinate them with subsecond precision, a seemingly implausible computational demand.
quotes.reason: The key objection to classical synapse-only models that motivates the whole theory

quotes.text: Spikes shape brain waves, while the waves in turn influence when and where spikes occur.
quotes.reason: Compact statement of the bidirectional mechanism at the heart of the theory

quotes.text: In this view, each neuron serves a stable, specialized function, i.e., a given neuron’s spikes always “mean” the same unique thing. The thought was that if we could decode each neuron’s message, their connections, and their collection into a functional patchwork of cortical areas, we could, in principle, understand the brain.
quotes.reason: Clear summary of the classical connectionist view being contrasted

quotes.text: An early example was the consistent finding that any given task engages around a third of all neurons in the prefrontal cortex (Asaad et al., 2000; Freedman et al., 2001; Wallis et al., 2001; Xiang et al., 2025). Under the traditional connectionist model, this would imply that we can only learn about three different cognitive functions before essentially all prefrontal neurons have been “assigned a function”, and its computational capacity is saturated.
quotes.reason: Concrete empirical finding that breaks the classical specialized-neuron model

quotes.text: A neuron might spike to object A, but only when it was seen first, and to object B, but only when it is seen second.
quotes.reason: Vivid concrete illustration of mixed selectivity

quotes.text: Because mixed selectivity neurons blend sensory, motor, and contextual information, they are inherently multifunctional, sending different messages in different situations. This indicates the cortex is not a mosaic of isolated, specialized, circuits of specialized areas. This means that cortical neurons have the capacity to participate in multiple networks, shifting membership as needed.
quotes.reason: States the implication that drives the need for a flexible routing mechanism

quotes.text: A control system therefore has the challenge of dynamically routing signals through a dense web of overlapping networks, allowing the same neurons to contribute to different computations in different contexts. Such flexible routing is difficult to reconcile with a purely connectionist framework based solely on changing synaptic weights. A more computationally tractable mechanism seems to be needed. Neural oscillations, i.e., brain waves, could serve that role.
quotes.reason: Pivotal transition linking the mixed-selectivity problem to the wave-based solution

quotes.text: Ephaptic coupling in the brain is the influence of neuronal electric fields on nearby neurons’ membrane potentials, allowing interaction and coordination independent of synapses
quotes.reason: Defines the key extra-synaptic mechanism the theory relies on

quotes.text: Individual ephaptic interactions, when synchronized and summed across neurons, create effects large enough to shape and coordinate neuron spiking at the mesoscale
quotes.reason: Core claim that ephaptic effects scale up to meaningful neural coordination

quotes.text: By contrast, changes in electric fields arise essentially concurrently with the underlying transmembrane currents and spread through the local tissue at the speed of electromagnetic propagation, making them effectively instantaneous on neuronal timescales
quotes.reason: Highlights the speed advantage of field-based signaling over synaptic transmission

quotes.text: Gamma rhythms are associated with net excitation and thus increased spiking, while alpha/beta rhythms are linked to reduced activity. In the motor cortex, for example, beta acts like a brake on movement execution. When alpha/beta decreases locally, gamma and spiking increase, and movement becomes more likely
quotes.reason: Establishes the push-pull relationship central to Spatial Computing theory

quotes.text: Gamma is highest in cortical superficial (feedforward) layers, while alpha/beta is strongest in deep (feedback) layers (Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2024).
quotes.reason: Key empirical anchor for the feedforward/feedback laminar organization of the two rhythms

quotes.text: Alpha/beta rhythms thus dampen or suppress gamma and associated spiking in targeted locations, creating a push-pull dynamic that determines where feedforward signals are suppressed. Feedforward signals are then permitted to emerge in the remaining “open” regions, where alpha/beta is weaker. Where spiking is expressed thus depends on the interaction between spatially random feedforward inputs and spatially organized alpha/beta suppression
quotes.reason: Full statement of the Spatial Computing mechanism

quotes.text: This scheme allows for flexible control over the neural expression of information in spiking, without the control system needing to know the precise neurons and synapses employed for any specific information
quotes.reason: Resolves the earlier-stated problem of implausible precision requirements

quotes.text: Alpha/beta rhythms reflected learned, internally generated contextual and categorical information, organized into spatial patterns across the cortical surface. These patterns inversely mirrored the spatial distribution of sensory information in spiking activity and predicted behavioral errors through mismatches in contextual representation.
quotes.reason: Empirical confirmation of the theory's predictions in real neural data

quotes.text: In this view, there is no requirement for specialized “context neurons” or “object neurons” with fixed tuning predicted by classical connectionists views of cortex. Instead, mixed selectivity arises from the interaction between broadly responsive neurons and mesoscale wave patterns that control when and where spiking is expressed.
quotes.reason: Direct contrast with the classical model, stating the theory's explanatory payoff

quotes.text: As traveling waves sweep continuously over the cortex, they may “pull” population spiking activity along, creating repeatable smooth trajectories
quotes.reason: Vivid image linking traveling waves to population-level dynamics

quotes.text: Rather than independent units driven solely by local, specialized connections, cortical populations behave like a coordinated flock governed by shared dynamics.
quotes.reason: Memorable metaphor capturing the shift from individual neuron view to population dynamics

quotes.text: We propose that one role of traveling waves, particularly in the alpha/beta band, may be in instantiating state changes in neural coding. That is, by moving patterns of inhibition vs excitation across the surface of cortex, alpha/beta waves can alter which subsets of neurons are permitted to spike and their correlational structure.
quotes.reason: States the theory's extension of Spatial Computing into the temporal/traveling-wave domain

quotes.text: Because the wave interactions occur everywhere simultaneously, the computation is inherently parallel. An analog system does not loop through variables but settles into a solution as a whole. This is in contrast to digital computing, which is inherently sequential, solving problems one step at a time.
quotes.reason: Explains why analog wave computation is efficient compared to digital computation

quotes.text: Their wave summation would essentially compute an intersection of constraints, resulting in a unique spatiotemporal pattern of neural activation for every possible combination of contexts
quotes.reason: Illustrates how analog wave computation could implement flexible combination of cognitive variables

quotes.text: The efficiency of analog computation could explain how the brain performs vast amounts of computation while consuming only about 20 watts, roughly the power of a dim light bulb (Kováč, 2010). By contrast, modern digital AI systems require enormous energy.
quotes.reason: Striking real-world comparison grounding the efficiency argument

quotes.text: Despite acting on different molecular targets, different anesthetic agents, such as propofol (GABAergic), ketamine (NMDAergic), and dexmedetomidine (alpha-2 adrenergic), all converge on similar large-scale electrical effects in the cortex
quotes.reason: Key evidence that consciousness depends on wave-level organization rather than specific molecular targets

quotes.text: This suggests that consciousness depends less on specific receptors or cell types and more on the integrity of large-scale wave organization.
quotes.reason: Direct conclusion drawn from the anesthesia evidence, central to the consciousness argument

quotes.text: Synaptic connections, shaped by experience, store long‑term information and define potential activity patterns. When neurons fire spikes, they generate electric fields that influence nearby neurons through ephaptic coupling, i.e., electrical interaction without direct synaptic contact. This creates a feedback loop: Synapses shape spiking, spiking contributes to brain waves, and waves shape spiking.
quotes.reason: Clear statement of the complementary synapse/wave framework that is the paper's synthesis

quotes.text: Moment‑to‑moment coordination underlying cognition and consciousness is thus dominated by brain waves rather than rapid synaptic changes.
quotes.reason: Blunt restatement of the paper's core claim near the conclusion

quotes.text: Brain waves can thus help solve the binding problem by dynamically linking distributed neural representations into a unified conscious experience.
quotes.reason: Connects the wave mechanism directly to the classic binding problem of consciousness

quotes.text: We, however, emphasize how this integration occurs via dynamic field interactions rather than broadcasting of information (GW) and spikes alone (GWNT).
quotes.reason: Pinpoints exactly how this theory diverges from Global Workspace Theory

quotes.text: Given strong evolutionary pressure to maximize computation per unit energy, it would be surprising if evolution did not exploit such a built‑in analog computing substrate.
quotes.reason: Closing evolutionary argument for why the brain would use wave-based analog computation

entries.name: Analog Computation
entries.senseHere: Solving a problem by letting continuous physical quantities, like overlapping wave patterns, combine and settle into an answer all at once, rather than stepping through calculations one at a time as a digital computer does. The article proposes that interfering brain waves perform this kind of computation, combining control signals from different contexts into a single new pattern of brain activity.

entries.name: Connectionism
entries.senseHere: The classical view that cortex works through hierarchical, feedforward networks of neurons, each tuned by its fixed synaptic connections to detect one increasingly complex, specialized feature. The article presents this as a good description of early sensory processing but incomplete for explaining flexible, context-dependent cognition.

entries.name: Mixed Selectivity
entries.senseHere: A single neuron's response to a stimulus changes depending on context, rather than always meaning the same thing. In the article's example, a neuron fires to one object only when it appears first in a sequence, blending object and order information together.

entries.name: Ephaptic Coupling
entries.senseHere: Neurons influencing each other's electrical activity directly through the field they create in surrounding tissue, without using synapses at all. The article treats this as the physical channel through which brain waves can speed up and coordinate spiking across many neurons at once.

entries.name: Gamma Oscillations
entries.senseHere: Fast brain waves (roughly 30-80 Hz) that the article links to increased neural firing and to carrying detailed, feedforward sensory and motor information over small patches of cortex.

entries.name: Alpha/Beta Oscillations
entries.senseHere: Slower brain waves (roughly 10-30 Hz) that the article treats as carrying top-down signals about goals and context, acting like a brake that suppresses firing in some locations, with movement or new information becoming possible where this brake weakens.

entries.name: Local Field Potential
entries.senseHere: The electrical signal picked up by an electrode placed inside brain tissue, reflecting the combined activity of many nearby neurons rather than any single cell. The article uses this as the measurable trace of the brain waves it argues help organize cognition.

entries.name: Spatial Computing
entries.senseHere: The article's proposed theory that slower alpha/beta waves form a spatial pattern across the cortex that suppresses faster gamma-driven spiking in some locations while sparing others, like a stencil. Where spiking is allowed to occur, rather than suppressed, depends on this overlap, and this is how context and goals are proposed to control which information gets expressed by neurons.

entries.name: Subspace Coding
entries.senseHere: The idea that a population of neurons, despite having huge numbers of possible firing patterns, tends to confine its actual activity to a much smaller, structured range of patterns, and that different kinds of information (like different contexts) are segregated into separate, non-overlapping ranges to avoid interfering with each other.

entries.name: Traveling Waves
entries.senseHere: Brain waves that sweep across the surface of the cortex in an organized direction, rather than staying in one place, altering the excitability of neurons as they pass. The article proposes these waves actively drive transitions between different patterns of neural activity, for instance when a stored memory is loaded or a representation changes.

entries.name: Phase-Amplitude Coupling
entries.senseHere: A pattern in which the strength of a faster brain wave rises and falls in step with the phase cycle of a slower wave, so the slow rhythm effectively paces the fast one. The article cites this as how theta waves organize and carry faster beta and gamma oscillations across the cortex.

entries.name: Global Workspace Theory
entries.senseHere: A rival theory holding that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely across a distributed brain network, making it available to many processes at once. The article agrees integration across cortex matters but argues this happens through interacting wave fields rather than through broadcasting of discrete signals or spikes alone.

entries.name: Integrated Information Theory
entries.senseHere: A rival theory of consciousness that locates it in how much a system's parts causally depend on and influence each other as an integrated whole, often pointing to a specific posterior brain region as critical. The article shares its emphasis on self-organization but places the relevant mechanism in large-scale wave dynamics rather than in one anatomical hot zone.

entries.name: Higher-Order Theories
entries.senseHere: Theories holding that a brain state becomes conscious only when another, higher brain state represents it, typically involving frontal cortex monitoring other areas. The article treats its own wave-based top-down organization as a physical mechanism for this kind of higher-order influence.

entries.name: Predictive Coding
entries.senseHere: A theory of brain function in which higher cortical areas continuously generate predictions about incoming sensory input and send them downward, with perception arising from comparing these predictions to actual input. The article treats its oscillatory top-down control as a physical implementation of this kind of predictive, higher-order influence.

entries.name: Nested Observer Model
entries.senseHere: A proposal that consciousness arises as a layered hierarchy, with different oscillatory rhythms each imposing organization on the level below them, rather than one single system observing the rest of the brain. The article aligns its own account of wave-based top-down organization with this layered picture.

events.label: Early finding: ~1/3 of prefrontal neurons engaged per task

dating.phrase: An early example was the consistent finding

occurrences.quote: An early example was the consistent finding that any given task engages around a third of all neurons in the prefrontal cortex (Asaad et al., 2000; Freedman et al., 2001; Wallis et al., 2001; Xiang et al., 2025).

Subsequently, it was confirmed that many cortical (and subcortical) neurons do indeed multiplex different kinds of information in their activity (Asaad et al., 2000; Warden and Miller, 2007; Cromer et al., 2010; Akam and Kullmann, 2014; Lankarany et al., 2019; Ramakrishnan et al., 2017; Rigotti et al., 2013).

events.label: Spatial Computing predictions confirmed in primates

occurrences.quote: We recently confirmed several key predictions of Spatial Computing theory by examining prefrontal cortex activity in non-human primates during complex cognitive tasks (Chen et al., 2026).

entries.text: Credentials and disclosures are settled first, before any claim about waves and mind begins.
Waves are proposed as the brain's missing executive; whether they truly replace synaptic control is still open.
Fixed, specialized neurons cannot explain cortex's behavior; something must flexibly reassign their function moment to moment.
Neurons that switch meaning by context need fast routing; oscillations and electric-field coupling are offered as how, not yet proven.
A concrete mechanism now appears: alpha/beta patterns gating faster signals, said to explain both shifting neurons and orderly populations.
Beyond gating, waves are claimed to compute outright, their overlaps producing new patterns rather than merely directing old ones.
Anesthesia data and rival theories test the claim: consciousness as organized wave integration, left as plausible but still unproven.
